title: A Dynamic Theory of Holdup
summary_en: When two parties make relationship-specific investments and then bargain over how to split the surplus, the famous holdup problem can lead to under-investment. Che and Sákovics put this in a fully dynamic model where investment and bargaining unfold over time. They show that, with sufficiently small bargaining frictions, the holdup problem essentially disappears: parties can invest efficiently because the option to keep negotiating disciplines opportunistic behaviour. The result reframes a long-standing puzzle in contract theory: holdup is a friction problem, not a structural one.
data_used: Theoretical paper. No data; results derived analytically from a dynamic bargaining-and-investment game.
policy_relevance: Underpins the design of long-term commercial contracts where neither party can credibly commit (infrastructure concessions, R&D joint ventures, supply contracts with relationship-specific capacity). Practical lesson for Hungarian public-procurement framing (KEHI / KFF) and PPP design: keeping renegotiation channels open with low transaction costs reduces under-investment, contrary to the intuition that strict ex-ante contracts are always better.
